pairs.rationale: Philippians calls the recipients my joy and crown while urging them to stand firm. Thessalonians calls the recipients the speakers' joy and crown of boasting before the Lord Jesus at His coming, and their glory and joy. The shared recipient-as-joy/crown image retains the different pronouns and coming context.

The next unit asks the true yoke-fellow to help these women, referring back to the named Euodia and Syntyche urged to think the same thing in the Lord. This is an internal continuation; it does not reconstruct a quarrel or identify the unnamed helper.

The preceding unit names Euodia and Syntyche, supplying the referents of these women in the request for help. The present unit adds their gospel striving with the speaker, Clement and other fellow workers. This identifies an antecedent without assigning Clement or the yoke-fellow a further identity.
Both direct rejoicing always. Philippians explicitly says in the Lord and repeats rejoice; Thessalonians gives the shorter command. The repeated formulation does not require an identical occasion.

Both relate conduct to the Lord's nearness. James explicitly says the Lord's coming has drawn near while urging patience and strengthened hearts; Philippians says the Lord is near after the gentleness instruction. This bounded comparison does not settle whether Philippians' shorter statement emphasizes presence, coming, or both.

Both join prayer with thanksgiving. Philippians directs requests to God in everything instead of anxiety; Colossians directs perseverance and watchfulness in prayer with thanksgiving. Their additional instructions remain distinct.

Both connect divine peace with the recipients' hearts. John records Jesus giving His peace and telling them not to let their heart be troubled or afraid; Philippians says God's peace will guard hearts and thoughts in Christ Jesus. The gift, guarding promise and named divine formulations are retained separately.

Philippians includes honorable things among the qualities readers are to consider. Corinthians speaks of taking care to do what is honorable before the Lord and people in administering a gift. This compares one named ethical quality without claiming that Corinthians repeats the whole list or the same mental instruction.

Both direct the community toward the speaker's own practice as a model. Corinthians appeals for imitation and sends Timothy to remind readers of the speaker's ways in Christ Jesus; Philippians tells readers to practice what they learned, received, heard and saw in him, with its God-of-peace promise. The different instructions and promises remain in their own passages.

The later acknowledgement of receiving the readers' provisions through Epaphroditus gives the gift context for their blossoming concern. This unit explicitly says they had been concerned but lacked opportunity; the later receipt does not imply that they previously felt no concern or supply a delivery date.

Both speak of contentment apart from accumulating possessions. Philippians says the speaker learned contentment whatever the circumstances; Timothy's letter calls godliness with contentment great gain and names food and coverings as sufficient. The personal learned response and the stated provisions are not identical claims.

Both describe the speaker's experience of hunger and hardship. Corinthians also lists labor, sleepless nights, thirst, fastings, cold and nakedness; Philippians contrasts hunger and need with fullness and abundance as conditions he has learned to face. The passages are not dated as the same incident.

Strength in the One who empowers is comparable to Corinthians' weak/strong contrast under Christ's power, amid hardships and distress. Philippians' unit does not explicitly name the empowering One, whereas Corinthians names Christ's power. Its all-things statement remains within the preceding fullness/hunger and abundance/need context.

Sharing in the speaker's affliction relates to the earlier description of the recipients sharing grace with him in chains and in the gospel's defense and confirmation. These internal partnership statements concern different named aspects of their relation, rather than an independently attested episode.

Both describe outside provision for the speaker's ministry, with Macedonia in the setting. Philippians limits its exclusive giving-and-receiving statement to the stated beginning/departure context; Corinthians speaks of wages from other Churches and brothers from Macedonia supplying his lack. It does not identify every donor as Philippian or date both statements to one occasion.

The because clause gives a concrete example of the preceding giving-and-receiving partnership: the Philippians sent once and twice for the speaker's need, with Thessalonica named. The preceding unit identifies the community and frames its exclusivity claim; no shipment dates or amounts are supplied.

Both use increasing-fruit language in connection with giving. Philippians seeks fruit increasing to the recipients' account rather than the gift itself; Corinthians says the One supplying seed will multiply it and increase the fruits of righteousness, with generosity producing thanks to God. The account and seed imagery remain distinct.

Both characterize sharing that pleases God through sacrifice language. Philippians calls the received provisions from the readers through Epaphroditus a fragrant aroma and acceptable sacrifice; Hebrews tells readers to do good and share because God is pleased with such sacrifices. Hebrews does not name this particular gift or messenger.

Both connect the community's provision with God's generosity. Philippians says God will fill their every need according to His riches in glory in Christ Jesus; Corinthians says God is able to make grace abound so that sufficiency enables every good work. The promise and statement of ability retain their different forms and purposes.

Both ascribe glory through the ages and conclude Amen. Philippians explicitly addresses our God and Father; Romans follows its from-Him, through-Him and to-Him statement about all things with glory to Him. Their fuller formulations remain distinct.

Both convey greetings from brothers and direct a greeting among the recipients. Philippians names every saint in Christ Jesus and the brothers with the speaker; Corinthians says all the brothers greet them and directs greeting one another with a holy kiss. The recipient descriptions and added kiss instruction differ.

Both say all the saints greet you. Philippians singles out those of Caesar's household, while Corinthians also directs a holy-kiss greeting. The shared closing formula does not identify individual household members or establish a writing location.

Both close with the Lord Jesus Christ's grace being with the recipients' spirit. Galatians also says our Lord, addresses brothers and includes Amen; Philippians preserves its shorter printed form. Those additions are not inserted into the source unit.
